output.summary: KEP-5677 adds a ResourcePoolStatusRequest API, modeled on the CertificateSigningRequest pattern, so users can see available DRA device capacity per pool. A controller in kube-controller-manager computes the result once per request and writes it to status; users recreate the request to refresh. The KEP is at implementable, stage alpha.
output.rationale: Users cannot easily see available versus allocated DRA capacity, and cross-namespace claims are hidden from less-privileged users. Earlier designs (per-pool status objects kept up to date by a controller, client-side kubectl tooling, and an out-of-tree extended API server) were rejected or reworked because of continuous etcd writes, RBAC exposure of claims, and connectivity issues. The request-object pattern computes on demand and keeps access under standard RBAC on the request.

alternatives.option: Controller-maintained ResourcePool objects auto-created for every pool
alternatives.why_not: Reviewers said the watches and writes needed to keep status for every pool are very high for something used only occasionally: "Imagine if we have multiple resource pools per node, and 10,000 nodes."

alternatives.option: Client-side utility only in kubectl, no control-plane object
alternatives.why_not: Users without cross-namespace ResourceClaim access cannot see usage, and reviewers noted that clients with old validation logic would misvalidate newer pools. Reviewer liggitt also disliked "synthetic" resources.

alternatives.option: Out-of-tree extended API server plus kubectl plugin
alternatives.why_not: The reviewers wanted in-tree, out-of-the-box support. The KCM debug endpoint option failed because kubectl has no existing way to reach KCM endpoints.

alternatives.option: Dedicated apiserver endpoint built into the API server
alternatives.why_not: pohly was not convinced it was acceptable: it adds overhead to a central component even when unused, and risks crashes there.

evidence.quote: This in-tree approach was chosen based on API review feedback to: - Provide an always-available, in-sync solution with Kubernetes releases
the number of watches and writes needed to maintain the status objects for every resource pool is likely very high, for something used only occasionally
It is a one-time operation with a timestamp. To recalculate, the user has to delete and recreate the object.
It gives us the ability to controller permissions on the object, too.
I don't think there are any blocker, except #6068 KEP update PR.
